title: Global supply chains

draft.title: Global supply chains
card: A transnational corporation is a business that operates in many countries. Many of them design, make and sell their products in different places.

A global supply chain is the series of steps, across many countries, that turns materials into a product in a shop. A phone may have its design in one country, its parts in a second and its assembly in a third.
Firms spread production to where it costs less, for example where wages are lower or skills are strong. This can lower the cost of making a product.
A long chain can be disrupted by events far away, such as a storm, a strike or a port closure. If one step stops, firms that rely on it may run short of parts.
draft.remember: Global supply chains can lower costs, but a problem at one step can disrupt the whole chain.

a.q: Why do many transnational corporations spread production across countries?
opts: To lower costs by making each step where it is cheaper
To avoid selling their products in other countries
To make sure no step can ever be disrupted
To use only materials found in their home country
a.why: Firms place each step where it costs less or where skills are strong, which can lower the cost of the product. A long chain is more exposed to disruption, not protected from it.
a.clue: Think about why a firm might choose where wages are lower.

b.q: A storm closes a port in Asia that ships parts for a bike maker in Adelaide. What is the most likely result?
opts: The maker runs short of parts and its production may slow
The maker finds its costs fall, as parts arrive faster
The maker is unaffected, as storms only affect nearby firms
The maker sells more bikes, as parts become scarce
b.why: The chain relies on that port, so a closure can stop parts arriving and slow production. Distance does not protect the firm, because the disruption was far away but still affected its supply.
b.clue: What happens to a factory when a needed part does not arrive?

a.best: To lower costs by making each step where it is cheaper

b.best: The maker runs short of parts and its production may slow

problems.detail: The right option is the only one with a qualifier ('may slow'). The others are stated flatly, so a student could pick it without knowing the idea.
The distractor 'storms only affect nearby firms' uses 'only'. Absolute wording like this marks the option as wrong, so students can rule it out without understanding supply chains.

Two distractors use absolutes: 'no step can ever be disrupted' and 'use only materials found in their home country'. These are easy to rule out on wording alone, which leaves the right option standing out.

check.summary: The card and both answers are accurate. However, absolute words ('only', 'ever') in the distractors, and the only hedged option in question b ('may slow'), let students guess the right answers from wording alone.

To make their supply chain shorter and simpler to run
